To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the critical cerebral perfusion pressures (CPP), determined by the dynamic intracranial and cerebrovascular pressure reactivity (iPRe) and cerebrovascular flow reactivity (CVRe), tests are 50 mmHgg, which is higher that that determined by the static autogulation curve, and that this discrepancy is caused by pathological microvascular shunts at high intracranial pressures.

the critical CPP, obtained by the static cerebral autoregulation test, is not valid with the intracranial hypertensive brain, and that the iPRx and CVRx tests accurately identify the CPP where the transition to pathological microvascular flow begins.

the critical cerebral perfusion pressures, obtained by static cerebral blood flow autoregulation curves and by dynamic intracranial and cerebrovascular pressure reactivity tests, differ with intracranian hypertension.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of novel methods to assess the critical CPP in intracranial hypertensive patients.
the assessment of dynamic cerebrovascular and intracranial ICP reactivity in impaired cerebrovascular autoregulation with intracranially increased ICP.
the dynamic assessment of impaired autoregulation in intracranial hypertensive brain.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the critical CPP is 50 mm Hg at high ICP and 60 mm Hg at low ICP.
the critical CPP for the brain is 50 mm Hg at high ICP.
the critical CPP for CBF autoregulation is 50 mm Hg in intracranial hypertensive rats.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
iPRx and CVRx are valid for the determination of the impaired critical CPP in the intracranial hypertensive brain.

dynamic CBF autoregulation tests are useful for the evaluation of impaired cerebrovascular autoregulation in intracranial hypertensive patients, and the critical CPP determined by the dynamic autoregulation test is higher than that determined by static autogregulation.
the critical CPP in intracranial hypertensive conditions should be defined by dynamic CBF reactivity tests.
The main takeaway from our work is that

dynamic tests of autoregulation are better than static tests in the presence of intracranial pathology, and that the critical CPP obtained by the static CBF autoregulation method should be re-evaluated.
iPRx and CVRx are more sensitive than static CBF autoregulation in detecting impaired autoregulation and critical CPP at high intracranial pressures.
dynamic CBF reactivity assessment of the impaired cerebrovascular autoregulation in the hypertensive brain is a more accurate method than the static CBF autoregulation assessment.
